newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain tempts unions with pay raise to avoid strike.
newsitem.headline: Spain tempts unions with pay raise to avoid strike.

text.p: Spain's conservative government has promised future pay raises to civil servants to coax them out of holding a general strike against a freeze on their 1997 salaries, the Public Administration Ministry said on Thursday.
A ministry spokesman said salaries would remain frozen in 1997, but the government had offered public workers raises in 1998 and 1999 in line with forecast inflation.
Spain's Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato told a conference on Wednesday that the government was going to do "everything possible" to avert a clash with workers.

But unions appeared determined on Thursday to take the government to task for its tough budget plan aimed at getting Spain in shape for European Monetary Union (EMU), and one leader said they would probably reject the latest offer.
"This is more of a provocation than an offer," Carlos Sanchez, a representative of the Workers' Commission (CCOO), one of Spain's two biggest unions, told state radio.
"This is not an offer that can provide a way out from the conflict...We will tell the government again that it has to modify the offer," he added.
Unions were meeting on Thursday to consider the proposal and will next hold talks with the government on December 3, the Public Administration Ministry said.

The government announced in July it would freeze public sector salaries in 1997 sparking mass protests. Labour leaders said they would continue their fight and would call a general strike in December if the government refused to back down.

The unions, led by the CCOO and the General Workers' Union (UGT), say the freeze violates a deal with the previous Socialist administration which guaranteed wages would rise in line with inflation in 1997.
They say government workers have lost 11.2 percent of their buying power since 1993, saving the government 785 billion pesetas ($6.09 billion) in the process.
Public sector pay was frozen in 1993 and increased a mere one percent in 1994, but moved up in line with inflation in 1995 and this year.

The Popular Party government, which made an election promise to push Spain into EMU, says the 1997 freeze is an essential part of its austere draft budget aimed at bringing the deficit down to the level required to join the single currency in 1999.
It estimates the measure will slash 200 billion pesetas off the deficit, helping to reduce it to three percent of gross domestic product in 1997 from a forecast 4.4 percent in 1996.
